translations.text: A sermon delivered by Apa John, archbishop of Constantinople, on repentance and self-control.
Blessed Paul, the apostle to the Gentiles, who became a teacher of the church, who struggled to equal the bodiless powers in his way of life,
Who finished the race and kept the faith,
Who shone through fasting, hunger, thirst, and dangers,
Who persevered on the journey from Jerusalem all the way to Illyricum, preaching the gospel,
This angel who belongs to earth,
And this man who belongs to heaven,
The one who has Christ speaking within him,
The dwelling place of the Holy Spirit,
Who was caught up to the third heaven and heard mysterious words,
Who was taken into paradise,
Whose love and zeal for Christ cannot be described,
The one who cares for the churches,
The spokesman for godliness,
The bridal escort of those who have believed in Christ,
The herald and teacher of the Gentiles,
Who showed us the way to ascend to heaven,
Said, “I discipline my body.
I make it a slave,
So that, after preaching to others, I myself may not be disqualified.”
If, then, this holy man, who possessed so many virtues, was the one who said with confidence, “I am not aware of anything I myself have done,”
Yet he was afraid and spoke this way,
Then what will we do, wretched people that we are, who have not achieved any virtue?
Should we not, then, stay alert and pray at all times,
And ask God not for gold or silver or any of this world’s wealth, but only for the wealth of heaven?
And that we may rejoice in the Lord.
Some rejoice in wealth,
others in places for drinking and in feasting,
and others in the beauty and glory of the world.
But let the virgin herself rejoice in the Lord.
And let her seek the honor that comes from him, saying, “My honor is with you.”
Nothing is as ugly or contemptible as a soul full of passion.
For this reason we ought to care for our soul
at all times, and say like Saint David, “Lord, give strength to my beauty,”
so that when the bridegroom beholds the soul’s beauty, he will say, “You are altogether beautiful, my companion, and there is no blemish in you.”
But even if you succeed in virtue, take care not to become proud of your beauty,
lest God turn his face away from you because of your pride.
For what can you do that is worthy of the things he endured for you?
He humbled himself for your sake; he gave his holy blood as a price for you.
He who feeds all flesh fasted in the flesh for your sake.
He who made the sweetness of honey,
tasted bitterness for your sake.
he who adorns heaven with the host of stars,
wore a crown of thorns for your sake,
having become obedient to the point of death—
death on a cross.
Therefore we ought not to boast about these things,
but to mourn and weep and listen to the one who says, “Grieve over what you say in your hearts upon your beds,”
so that we may remember at night the things we have done during the day and sigh over them.
This is what Ahab did when he was grieved:
he fasted and wrapped himself in sackcloth.
And what did the Lord say about him? “I will not bring disaster upon him during his lifetime.”
For this very reason, the Savior called those who weep blessed.
Not those who weep over damage or the loss of money,
but over their sins.
You too should say, like David, “I will soak my bed every night.
I will drench my couch with my tears.” And again, “My eyes have poured out streams of water because they have not kept your law.” Wash away the stain with tears.
Beat your breast.
Remind yourself of your sins.
that you committed.
You were once ensnared through your eyes.
You once opened your eyes to evil.
You harmed your soul through your eyes.
The eyes that looked at evil—
heal them now with tears.
And close your eyes so that you do not look at worthless things again,
lest you fall into an evil habit.
For habit drags whoever follows it down into great sins.
When you are wearing a beautiful garment, you take care not to sit down just anywhere, lest it become stained.
For if you disregard the first stain, the second, and the third, then, since the whole garment is stained,
you no longer hesitate to sit down anywhere dirty.
What, then, shall we do? What is needed now is powerful prayer,
lest you strike your foot against a stone,
and so that the angel of the Lord may encircle you and rescue you, and you too may be able to say, “The angel who rescues me from every evil.”
And so that the angel may call to you too from heaven, as he did to Abraham.
For the angels themselves love those who love their Lord.
He said, “Take up a psalm and sound a tambourine.”
A sweet-sounding psaltery and a lyre.
You receive one, but three are demanded of you.
For we are composed of three, as the apostle says: “May he preserve your spirit whole, together with your soul and your body.”
The psaltery is the spirit.
The lyre is the soul.
But the tambourine has a dead skin stretched over it.
So put the flesh to death,
so that you may be able to praise the Lord with a tambourine and dancing.
For the Lord himself burned the flesh for your sake.
Take care lest he say to you, “What profit is there in my blood?”
What, then, will you give in return to the one who endured all these sufferings for your sake?
Become a fruit-bearing tree, so that the Lord’s blessing may rest upon you.
Bear fruit according to your ability.
If you cannot produce a hundred, which is perfection, at least produce sixty, which is half.
If this is difficult for you, at least produce thirty, which is a third,
Only act according to your ability,
lest you be fruitless, and they cut you down and throw you into the fire.
If you will not be a vessel of gold or silver, do not become wood, grass, or straw either, for these are fuel for the fire.
Do not do the deeds that God hates, lest they stand against you on the day of judgment like an image,
and you then begin to confess them there without a witness,
without an accuser, without proof,
as you behold everything you have done,
together with everything you have said carelessly, depicted before your eyes.
Weep before the time comes, lest you hear there, “This is not the time to repent.”
For there is no repentance in this place.
As long as we have time, let us work.
If time slips away from us,
there is no way for us to find another opportunity.
For this reason, then, blessed Paul teaches us, saying, “As long as we have time, let us do what is good.”
And again, “Look, now is the acceptable time.”
Let us weep over the evil deeds we have done.
Let our tears flow down our cheeks. Let us beat our breasts,
so that we may escape the weeping and gnashing of teeth in the place to which we will go.
Let us also weep like David,
so that we may be called blessed. He did not merely weep casually like this.
Rather, he soaked his bed with his tears, keeping vigil through the night.
It was on a single night that he sinned.
Yet he wept every single night of his whole life, confessing these words
of this kind before God: “Lord, forgive me, for you gave me my eyes so that I might see the light with them.
But I used them to look at evil.
Since, then, I went astray through my eyes,
I therefore wash away my sins with tears.”
Let us leave our evil habits behind and move up to the city in heaven.
Let us discipline our body and make it a slave, so that we do not make our soul a slave to the devil.
Let meditation on God's words drive away the pleasures that dwell within us,
which are like wild beasts,
as we always carry the death of our Lord Jesus Christ in our body.
Let us remember the one who said, “Be sober and stay awake.”
Let no one receive a crown while sleeping.
Let no one receive prizes while being neglectful and snoring.
Rather, the one who endures blows and bitter suffering is the one who will receive honor from the judge of the contest.
The enemy flees from the one who is alert, but plunders the one who is asleep.
For this reason, you have realized that you have evil enemies.
Do not give sleep to your eyes,
or slumber to your eyelids,
so that you may escape like a gazelle from a snare and like a bird from a trap.
Let us always flee from the cares of this life and its snares.
Since we have renounced the world, let us not concern ourselves again with worldly things.
For the deceiver's traps are many.
He said, “Your adversary, the devil, walks around roaring like a lion, seeking not merely to seize possessions,
but to swallow up your souls.”
Flee from the deceiver's cunning,
and say, “Through you I will escape a band of robbers,
and through my God I will leap over a wall.”
Do not refuse suffering, lest you refuse the crown.
A merchant does not bring in profits without enduring waves to obtain goods.
The wrestler who competes endures blows while looking forward to the crown.
A farmer does not find sheaves unless he first sows the seeds through his own labor.
This is how those who await the kingdom of heaven regard afflictions as nothing, their hearts burning with hope for the good things to come.
Therefore, let us pay attention and remain watchful at all times, for our bridegroom will suddenly look out from the bridal chamber,
so that when we hear his voice, we may get up and meet him, ready.
For he said, “Keep your belts fastened and your lamps burning, and be like people waiting for their master.”
Look, even now the Savior calls the vigilant person blessed, saying, “Blessed is that servant whom his master finds keeping watch when he comes.”
Just as he calls those who keep watch blessed,
so he regards the negligent person as wretched,
saying, “If that wicked servant says in his heart, ‘My master will be delayed,’ and begins to beat his fellow servants and to eat and drink with drunkards,
that servant's master will come on a day he does not know and at an hour he does not expect. He will cut him in two and assign him his share with the unbelievers.”
If the person who says, “My master will be delayed,” will be cut in two, what will they do to someone who does not expect him at all?
So, my beloved, we ought to be found ready at all times for the single [?], which comes only once.
For there is no way for us to return again and set right what we have neglected.
So let us be ready at all times, so that we can say boldly, “God, my heart is ready; my heart is ready.”
We are in a great war in this life.
The sinners, who are the demons, have drawn their bow.
One shoots arrows at our ears so that we will listen with pleasure to slander.
Another shoots at our eyes to make us look with evil intent at things we should not.
Another shoots at our tongue to make us insult our brother.
And another shoots at our stomachs, stirring us to gluttony.
Another shoots at our hands, drawing us toward robbery and a greedy desire for more.
Yet another stirs our feet to make them walk toward evil.
Because of all these things, the blessed Paul strengthens us.
He wrote, “Take up the full armor of God and the helmet of the Spirit,
with which you will be able to extinguish every burning arrow of the evil one.”
Let us listen to the voice of the prophet, who says, “You have been told, human being, what is good.
And what does the Lord ask of you except to practice justice and righteousness,
to love mercy, and to be ready to follow the Lord your God?”
So let us forget what lies behind and stretch forward toward what lies ahead.
Let us nourish ourselves in the Lord and delight in his words.
Let us not waste time standing around like this, aimlessly and for nothing. Instead, since we have our Lord, let us serve him in truth.
Look at his great love for us: sometimes he encourages us,
and sometimes he threatens us with punishments.
At other times he teaches us obedience, promising a reward to those who obey him.
Therefore, having girded the loins of our hearts with truth,
let us serve the good Lord, our Savior.
Let us remember everything he underwent for our sake.
He was born as a human being for our sake.
He was cared for as a human being; he was a young child.
He was baptized for our sake.
He went hungry; he slept; he forgot for our sake.
He grieved, and people plotted against him.
They whipped him and humiliated him.
Finally, they handed him over to death for us.
So let us always reflect on the one who endured all these things for our sins.
“You have not yet reached the point of shedding blood,” he said.
“But you are struggling against sin.” This means that we are not now being required to give our blood for Christ.
Rather, a sinless life is being sought from us.
Remember also our Savior’s acts of healing: he healed the sick.
He cast out demons and made the lame walk.
He made the blind see, along with all the other things that it is not our task to recount one by one.
As the culmination of all these things, he graciously gave us the way to ascend to heaven, so that we too might follow him through a life of virtue and gain our citizenship in heaven,
as befits the place where our name has been recorded.
Scripture called us strangers and foreigners so that we would look down on the things of this world.
Pleasure is like a dog.
If you chase it away, it runs away; but if you feed it, it stays with you.
That is why James said, “Stand against the devil, and he will flee from you.”
Let us not think that we can repent in Hades.
For the medicine of repentance has no power in that place.
Rather, even if we gnash our teeth and our tongue burns, there is no one there who will dip his finger in water for us.
Instead, we too will hear the words that this rich man heard.
Since we understand, my beloved, that the affairs of this world are no different from dreams, and that we are staying in an inn that we must certainly leave,
let us give thought to the journey and the provisions we will take with us on the road.
As we leave this life, let us put on the clothes that Paul advised us to wear, saying, “Clothe yourselves with heartfelt compassion, kindness, and humility.”
We do not need gold in that place; it is a drop of water that we need.
We do not need leaves, but fruit. We do not need words, but deeds.
For he said, “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father in heaven.”
So let us not deceive ourselves.
Even if someone spends their whole lifetime eating and drinking, it is nothing compared with the endless ages.
For here, both good things and bad things come to an end.
But in that place there are good things that last forever, and punishments without end.
Here, even if the body burns, the soul comes out unharmed.
But in that place, even though the body rises imperishable, the soul is burned continually.
For sinners too must rise imperishable, not so that they may receive glory, but so that they may be tormented without dying.

If we cannot bear the hot air of a bathhouse when it is not heated beyond the proper temperature, what will we do when we are handed over to the river of fire that flows before Christ’s judgment seat?
For everyone must be tested by that fire.
Let us examine the seal to see whether our gold is safe, or whether our treasure has been plundered.
For all our deeds are exposed to the one who will call us to account, and there is no way to deceive that judge.
While we still have time, come, let us heal the wounds of our soul with tears.
If the prophet Jeremiah wept over the destruction of the temple,
which was built of actual stones, saying, “Let me weep bitterly,” how much more should we weep over our own temple, which is far more precious,
in which there is not a golden [?], but the Holy Trinity dwells.
If, when we see someone who has died, we weep over them out of habit,
then who could be so utterly senseless as not to weep over their own soul when it has died through sin?
Therefore, you should not weep over a corpse, but over the death of your soul.
Remember that the time has drawn near.
And the judge is standing at the door. The night has advanced, and the day has drawn near.
Let no one remain asleep when the night passes and the sun rises.
So let us wake up from the sleep of dreams. Let us produce fruit worthy of repentance, as it is written.
Repentance does not require a long time, and many of the martyrs received the crown in a short time.
Even if we have committed sins that lead to death, let us not give up on ourselves. For we have remedies that bring salvation: our tears.
For it is human nature to stumble in something.
But persisting in stumbling is the work of Satan.
For falling is not what is bad; rather, failing to rise from the fall is what is evil and destructive.
For this reason our Lord cried out to us through the prophet: “Is there no balm in Gilead?
“Or is there no physician there?
“Why, then, has healing not come to the daughter of my people?”
Now, if a part of our body becomes sick, we look for physicians and make every effort until we have healed the sick part of our body.
But when our soul is sick, we neglect it and take no care at all for its salvation.
Let us fear the one who has the power to destroy our soul and our body in Gehenna.
Come, let us run to the ocean of God's mercies before the time of torments.
And let us too say with Saint David: “You will sprinkle me with it, and I will become whiter than snow.”
The good shepherd stands ready, wanting to snatch our souls from the lion's mouth before it swallows them.
He calls out to us too: “My son, have you sinned? Do not do it again.”
And: “Does someone fall and not get up?
“Or does someone turn away and not turn back again?”
And: “Return to me, children who have gone astray, and I will heal your wounds.”
The one who said, “I did not come to judge the world, but so that the world might be saved through me,” does not lie.
Only let us repent.
For he said, “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but rather that the sinner turn away from his evil path and live.”
No one among those who love bodies, even if he burns with passion for the woman he loves, can love her so much.
How God loves the soul that repents
And he called to the woman who had prostituted herself many times, saying, “And I said to her, after she had prostituted herself in all these ways, ‘Return to me.’”
For such is God’s love for humanity.
He never turns away from anyone who turns his mind toward him in repentance,
even if that person has fallen into the mud of evil. Instead, he stretches out his hand to him, saying, “Return to me, and I will save you.”
And again, “On the day when you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts.”
For if a physician, even when the sick person becomes discouraged and insults him,
does not despise him or retaliate against him for the insults, but treats him gently,
how much more will the good God, the true physician of our souls!
Only let us not give up on our own salvation.
For often a wrestler falls during the contest, but in the end gets up and wins the crown.
And a soldier, after being wounded and treated, fights again and gains greater distinction than those who have never been wounded at all.
And many merchants, after their ship sinks and they lose their cargo, do not give up.
Instead, they return to trading again and become rich.
For was the fire of Gehenna prepared for us? No! It was prepared for the devil and his angels.
Only let us not kindle that fire against ourselves, and then hear in turn, “Go into the flame that you have kindled.”
No illness is incurable with the medicine of the physician of our souls.
But perhaps you will say, “I cannot reach perfection.”
If you cannot reach perfection, if you cannot become like the sun, at least become like the stars.
Only move from earth up to heaven, and become like the stars that shine.
It is better for you to do a few good deeds than to do nothing at all.
You have been told about pouring water [?], and about visiting the sick and those in prison.
For if we will be punished for our words and our thoughts,
how much more will he reward us for our good deeds, even if they are small!
So then, let us toil for a little while, so that we do not fall short of eternal life.
For if it were possible for us to die many times, we ought to do so, until we see Christ coming in his glory.
We will not see him through a riddle, but will behold him as he is,
with our own eyes, according to the testimony of the apostle John, who speaks about God.
If we marvel at the beauty of a body here when we see it,
even though the beauty of bodies comes from fluids and phlegm, and after death they become worms, [?], and dust,
how much more when we behold that beauty which is imperishable, unchanging, and undefiled!
Peter saw only a tiny ray of the light of his glory.
He said to us, “It is good for us to stay here.”
What, then, will happen to us when we behold all that glory?
If we consider those close to an earthly king fortunate when we see him coming out on his golden chariot, wearing his crown and purple robe,
then how much more blessed will we be if we are placed at the right hand of the King of all, the judge of everyone!
Suppose you had been promised a kingdom, but the road to the country where the kingdom lay was difficult and rough,
with rocky ground and steep places. Would you not endure all these things until you gained that kingdom?
Do not say, “I have already been caught in my sins. I cannot turn back to God.”
Even if the devil has already thrown us down, let us get up quickly.
For our Lord loves humanity.
He will run out to meet us and welcome us, just as he did for the young son who squandered his share of the property.
Let us remember that after Solomon became king and experienced all the splendid things of this life,
he said, “Emptiness upon emptiness is what is in them all.”
If rulers make every effort to be honored by those sitting in the theaters, even though most of those there are poor, despised people, slaves, and foreigners,
then how much more should we strive to be acclaimed in that theater, the place where the angels, the archangels, and all the saints are gathered!
Let us not allow sexually immoral people and tax collectors to enter the kingdom before us.
There are many remedies and means of help provided for us in holy Scripture, differing from one another.
Ahab grieved over the sin he had committed and escaped God's wrath through this remedy; Nebuchadnezzar through mercy.
The people of Nineveh escaped through this remedy of fasting.
The prostitute reconciled God to herself through her tears.
The robber became a citizen of paradise through faith.
Having taken up these poultices and these medicines,
let us treat our souls for the wounds of sin that we inflict on ourselves.
Let us too say before the true physician, “Heal me, Lord, and I will be healed,” and, “Heal my soul, for I have sinned against you.”
And the true physician will welcome us and say, “I, I am the one who wipes away your sins, and I will not remember them.”
You have seen this abundance of medicines and these various remedies, which the physician has mercifully provided for us against the various bites and wounds.
Choose whichever of these you want for the healing of your soul.
If you cannot give alms like Nebuchadnezzar, at least grieve over your sins like Ahab. If you cannot fast like the people of Nineveh,
at least wash away your sins with your tears like the prostitute. Run to the merciful one, saying with David, “Have mercy on me, God, according to your great mercy.”
It was not a snake that bit me, so that I should run to a snake charmer, nor was I stained with mud, so that I should wash myself with water.
Rather, it was the devil who cast his venom upon me, and I was stained with the mud of my lawlessness.
That is why I need the great mercy of your love for humanity.
Only turn your heart toward him and ask him,
and the Father of spirits will graciously give you the Spirit. He is the one who said, “If the lawless person turns away from his evil way, I will not remember any of the lawless deeds he has done.”
Only uncover your wound before him and say, “Have mercy on me. Have mercy on my body and my soul.
Have mercy on me in this age and in the next.
Have mercy on me because of the weakness of nature and because of the ocean of your goodness.”
Only desire healing, and the physician will take the initiative with his medicines.
For he seeks your salvation. He is the one who brought back the sheep that had gone astray.
He is the one who sent his servant out onto the roads so that they would invite the wicked and the good to the wedding.
Look, he offers you too the kingdom of heaven.
If you cannot buy it with money, buy it for yourself with little pieces of bread. He gives you the kingdom of heaven in exchange for these.
Look, the prophet cries out, saying, “Who is the person who desires life, who loves to see good days?” And, “You who have no money, go and buy for yourselves.”
For what does the giver ask for? We have no money to give.
If not, offer a ransom for your soul: offer fasting; offer tears.
If you have none of these other things, then restrain your tongue from evil and your lips from speaking deceit.
This will be the beginning of your soul’s salvation. But pay attention to yourself.
Even if you fast, guard yourself against becoming proud.
Even if you give alms, do not do it for praise from people.
Rather, when the day of fasting passes, examine yourself and see what you have gained for yourself through fasting, lest you be found to be just as you were before you fasted.
Instead, see which sin you have left behind, or in what you have made progress.
What good achievement have you gained for yourself?
Or what weakness have you corrected through fasting?
See whether you have withdrawn from anger and left rage behind.
See whether you have stopped insulting others, slandering your brother, and plotting evil against your neighbor.
See whether you have stopped swearing oaths and speaking foolish words, idle words, or chatter.
See what good you have gained for yourself.
If you have abstained only from bread and other foods, but have not abstained from the passions or acquired virtues for yourself, then what have you gained through fasting?
Do not say, “So-and-so insulted me; I too will insult him.
So-and-so ruined my reputation;
I too will ruin his. So-and-so treated me unjustly;
I too will take revenge on him.”
Instead, leave room for the true judge, who will repay each person according to their deeds.
For all these things will be revealed and examined in that arena where the whole world will gather,
in the place where no one will be able to help another and rescue them from the sentence that cannot be appealed.
In that place of judgment, neither Moses nor Noah nor Daniel nor even Abraham, who loves his children, will be able to save a single one of his children from punishment.
Let us remember that we are guilty of many sins, both hidden and openly visible.
For he said, “If you keep track of sins, who will be able to stand?”
And why am I speaking about hidden sins?
If he judges us for those that are openly visible, what forgiveness will there be for us?
If he examines us or questions us about our carelessness in our prayers and our faintheartedness,
or about what we are arranging as we stand before [?], or what we are thinking about,
we do not give him even the kind of honor that slaves give their masters,
or that soldiers give their commanders, or that friends give their friends.
For when we speak with our friends, you will find us paying close attention to them. But when we pray to God about our sins, we do so carelessly.
And you will indeed find our knees bent down, while our minds are imagining the affairs of the world.
If he questions us about this alone, where will we be able to stand?
And what will we do if he brings forward the accusations we make against one another, along with our jealousy and hatred?
What will we do if he examines us about our malicious looks and questions us about our evil desires?
If he demands an account of our mockery, will we be able to open our mouths?
And if he judges us for our love of human praise, which we have mixed with our prayers, our fasting, and our acts of mercy,
will we be able to look up to heaven at all?
If he examines us about the deceptions we devise against one another—when our brother is with us, we speak to him as a friend,
but when he is away from us, we accuse him as though he were an enemy—
and if he calls us to account for our false oaths, our lies, our groundless anger toward one another, and our envy,
and for the way we become upset when we see one of our companions enjoying a good reputation or receiving more honor than we do, and the way we rejoice over others when misfortune overtakes them,
how much punishment will we be liable to for things like these?
If he calls us to account for our carelessness in our gatherings—for our Lord himself is speaking to us through the Scriptures,
but we turn away from him and speak with our fellow servants—
how great a punishment will we be liable to for behavior like this?
Therefore, let us keep Gehenna before our eyes at all times.
Even if we had never been threatened with Gehenna at all, we ought to remember our sins at all times. How much more so when it stands ready for us!
Remember your judge, then.
For look, he has told you about the punishment in advance so that you may escape the danger.
If he commands you to fast, you find an excuse because of your weakness.
If he tells you, “Give alms,” you find an excuse because of your poverty.
If he tells you, “Do not store things up here,” you find an excuse because of your concern for your children.
If he tells you, “Do not be angry, do not be envious, do not hate, do not despise your neighbor,” you will say, “Who [?] in the face of these things?”
So you have no defense, nor will you receive forgiveness for things of this kind. How will you be able to lift your hands toward heaven while these things are in your soul?
But often you will say, “They treated me unjustly. They deprived me of my possessions. They harmed me. They spoke evil of me.”
Then bear it and wait for the ruler’s judgment.
For if a slave insults you, you do not strike him, but you report him to his master.
How much more ought you to leave room for the one who said, “Leave judgment to me; I will repay, says the Lord.”
For you know that you must be made to stand before a fearsome judgment seat, where neither an advocate nor money will be able to help you,
and that your soul will pass through the river of fire that flows before the judgment seat of Christ.
Send a father ahead of you to that place.
Let the fountain of your tears match the measure of the sins you have committed.
If your sin is small, then a little weeping is enough.
If your transgression is great, then you also need torrents of tears.
But if you are free from sin, lend your tears to your brother and weep with him over his sins.
The place through which sin entered is the eyes.
Let healing also come through that same place.
Let us repent before the door of repentance is shut against us.
Therefore, let the one who says, “I am standing,” take care that he does not fall.
But let the one who has slipped and fallen hurry to get up, and do not let him give up on himself.
For it is written, “The Lord raises up those who have fallen.”
Sometimes a person is shaken a little, as Saint David said: “As for me, my feet almost slipped; my steps almost gave way.”
And again: “When I say, ‘My foot has slipped,’ your mercy, Lord, helps me.”
Then again: “They pushed me to make me fall, but the Lord helped me.”
The one who has fallen also has encouragement not to remain fallen. He said, “Does someone fall and not get up?”
But be careful that hearing about the Lord’s goodness does not make you careless.
It is also written, “God is a true judge, strong and patient.”
In his love for humanity, he accepts the repentance of those who turn back to him.
But he said, “If you do not turn back, he will sharpen his sword.”
Notice that he said, “He will sharpen it.”
But he does not strike yet, so that, when you see that he has sharpened the sword,
you may act before the sentence is passed, and fear may awaken you to repentance.
For he said, “He has bent his bow and made it ready.”
But since you have not yet been [?] by the arrow, do not despise the judge’s patience.
Listen to the Savior’s patience when he says, “Come to terms with the one taking you to court.” Your adversary, or the one fighting against you, is with you at all times.
You cannot separate yourself from him. Paul will explain him to you when he says, “For the flesh desires what is against our spirit, and the spirit what is against the flesh.”
These, then, oppose one another.
The spirit opposes the flesh, uprooting worldly desire through hope in the kingdom of heaven.
The flesh, in turn, opposes the spirit, inclining toward the earth and its pleasures.
Therefore, come to terms with the one taking you to court while he is with you on the road.
For once the road comes to an end, you will no longer find another opportunity to repent.
Be careful that the one taking you to court does not hand you over to the judge,
and the judge hand you over to the officer—that is, the merciless powers in charge of punishments—and they throw you into prison, which is the outer darkness, until you pay the last penny.
For you will be judged not only for your deeds, but also for your thoughts and plans.
Since we understand all these things, then, let us help ourselves.
When we experience punishment, then we will understand that pleasure is bitter and becomes a source of intense bitterness for us.
Since this is how things stand, my beloved, let us plead with the merciful God not to hand us over to the demons,
saying, together with the holy David, “Do not hand me over to those who oppress me.”
For they are the ones urging us into sin now.
They are also the ones who will become our accusers on the day of judgment.
For not only the devil himself, but all the other demons too will accuse us, saying, “Was it not we who served you in sexual immorality,
and anger, and the love of empty glory, and slander?”
Let us fear that day, that hour when our own thoughts will become harsh judges against us,
and all that we have [?] will stand against us, depicted before us like a picture.
Let us plead with our Lord with all our heart.
For even though we are clothed in weak flesh, the one who is ready to help us and save us, bringing us into his kingdom, is great.
We [?] for three reasons: either because of his goodness, or because he too loves us, or because of his beauty.
What other beauty, then, compares with that of our Lord?
As David says, “He is more beautiful in his appearance than the sons of men.”
Who, then, does good as he does? He has prepared for those who love him good things that no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and that have never entered a human heart.
Who, then, can love us in this way, as our Lord and Father does?
He cries out, “Will a mother forget her children?
Or will a bride forget the adornment she wears?
Or will a virgin forget the sash tied around her? But I will not forget them,” says the Lord.
Look at blessed David and the way he longs to see the Lord. He said, “When will I come and appear before the face of my God?”
He did not want to wait until the appointed end of his lifetime, but burned to leave this place and see the one he loved.
Truly, such love or such yearning belongs to a wise soul that has taken wing and is flying toward heaven.
You too, love him alone, and pass by all the affairs of this life as though they were shadows.
Remember eternal life at all times:
the kingdom that endures, dancing with the angels, and the glory of incorruptibility,
and life with Christ, in which there is no anguish. He said, “Anguish has fled, along with sorrow and sighing.”
Reflect on this life: there is nothing in it but sorrow, weeping, anguish, contempt, neglect, sin, hardship, old age, and death.
David, then, was contemplating these things, and things worse than these—bereavement and widowhood,
untimely deaths, punishments, and all the rest of the afflictions that prevail in this life—
and he longed to be free of them all.
He said, “When will I come and appear before my God?”
He wanted to leave this place and go to the place where there are peace, joy, love, and splendor,
and freedom from worry, and all the other good things that no words can describe.
Therefore, since you too hope to enjoy such delight, do not be careless.
Instead, let your lamp always be burning, and be ready to meet the bridegroom,
so that you too may hear, “Enter into the joy of your Lord.”
We must keep watch and pray at all times.
For if, after God said to the devil, “Do not touch my servant Job,”
he continued hoping to bring him down, how much more will he not struggle against us, who are within his reach,
to bring us down? We need a continual vigil to guard our souls.
For a soldier often keeps vigil on journeys, and a fisherman does not sleep, but stays awake and keeps watch all night until he catches a great many fish.
Likewise, the farmer keeps vigil so that nothing will damage his vineyard. In the same way, the shepherd keeps vigil, guarding his flock of sheep,
like the patriarch Jacob, who said, “I was burning in the heat by day and in the frost by night, and sleep fled from my eyes.”
What is the reward for such vigils? “So that,” he said, “a wild animal would not destroy even a single sheep.”
If he takes such great care over an unreasoning sheep, how much care ought we to take over our rational soul, which is more precious than anything else,
which will be made to stand before a fearful judgment seat to give an account of everything it has done?
Therefore, let us remove the burden of our sins from ourselves before reaching the place of judgment.
For there is no opportunity for us to repent in that place.
That is why our departure from the body has been arranged to remain hidden from us, so that we may be afraid at all times.
If, in the court here, those appointed to be tried become agitated and grow rigid with fear when they hear the herald’s voice calling out,
how much more will those appointed to stand before the fearful judgment seat, amid thousands upon thousands and tens of thousands upon tens of thousands of angels!
Look at the blessed Jacob: when he placed a stone under his head and went to sleep, he saw a ladder on the earth whose top reached up to heaven,
and the angels and God were going up and coming down on it,
carrying the prayers up before God and bringing us gifts from him.
We must therefore contemplate all these things.
Rather, they will grieve over us.
If they rejoice when they see us repenting, in the same way they also grieve over our negligence.
For our conscience always finds fault with us, tormenting us over what we have done, especially when we speak about the judgment to come.
Yet rebuke through good words is good.
If only they had rebuked that rich man instead of burning his tongue in a fire that cannot be extinguished!
You desire virginity. If you keep the commandments, the Lord will grant it to you.
For if you say in prayer, “Guard me, Lord, like the pupil of an eye,” he in turn will say to you, “Guard my words and my commandments like the pupils of your eyes.”
When you keep his commandments, he in turn will care for your soul, and you will say concerning yourself, “Whoever touches you is like someone touching the pupil of his eye.”
Now then, beloved, you have put your hand to the plow. Do not turn back; do not become like a pillar of salt.
Let your tongue always speak about the judgment to come, so that you may benefit and become an excellent person through fear of that place of judgment.
Do not let anger, sorrow, or any other passion rule over you, so that you utter rash words without examining them.
Instead, let the law of the Lord always be in your mouth, so that through all these things your eyes may be opened.
And let your words be in accordance with the law of God.
Keep the lawgiver always before your eyes. Let him dwell with you and be your counselor.
Even if you see someone living luxuriously and enjoying great wealth, understand that he will quickly wither like grass.
Let him delight in food; you, for your part, delight in the words of the Lord.
Many virgins became martyrs. If those women conquered death,
should you, for your part, as a man, not conquer lust?
Strive to make your limbs bronze, so that you may not only conquer lust,
but also restrain yourself from wrath and anger.
Let the tongue have its limits.
Take care not to let your conscience condemn you before the judgment.
Remember that all our deeds must be revealed.
We do not want even a single person here to see us behaving shamefully.
Where, then, will we hide in that place, among thousands of thousands and tens of thousands of tens of thousands?
John, because he was a holy virgin, reclined on Jesus’ chest.
Likewise, let the soul that wishes to become the bride of Jesus Christ preserve its purity, so that the tree may be recognized by its fruit.
The righteous person professes faith openly.
Always remember the good confession of Christ, taking the remembrance of the last day into your heart. Guard yourself on every side, especially your tongue.
He said, “The tongue is what defiles the whole body.” When the body is defiled, the heart must also be corrupted along with it.
Paul therefore rightly said, “People whose hearts are corrupted.” Evil words corrupt good hearts.
Seek Paul as blessed Thecla did, so that you may hear Paul’s words.
You need wings. But if you have no wings, then you have promised to fly up on high.
Let your eyes look downward, but let your heart be in the heights of heaven.
You need great vigilance, for your adversary stands against you, wide awake.
He threw him out of the paradise on earth. Now that he sees you ascending to heaven, he will not neglect his task.
Listen to the one who says, “I want you to be free from worry.”
Have no worry at all except concern for the kingdom of heaven alone.
If you desire to ascend from earth to heaven with your body, subdue the flesh through fasting and make it light, so that it may rise easily to the heights.
For when a horse eats too much, it cannot run or even walk in an orderly way; instead, it becomes unruly. And if Israel had not eaten, he would not have kicked.
Lift your eyes to heaven, [?] the spirit in which the one who moves it is, and overcome the passions through holy truth.
Prayer and faith will help you. Holy Scripture teaches you. Already here you have the pledge of the resting places in heaven.
You do not live with a wife who causes you to stumble. You are not concerned about children. You have been freed from the worry of raising children.
Follow your Lord, who leads you into the kingdom of heaven.
Follow the one who says to you, “If you walk uprightly toward me, I too will walk uprightly toward you.”
If you want to become like Christ, follow in his footsteps.
The gate is narrow and constricted. The righteous are the ones who enter through it.
Listen to blessed Daniel saying, “I, Daniel, was mourning for three weeks.
I ate no desirable bread, and neither meat nor wine entered my mouth.”
John, while living in the wilderness, did not acquire a vineyard for himself, so that he would make himself barren.
As for you, let these things be ready to instruct you.
You have chosen for yourself a way of life that belongs to heaven.
Fight the good fight of faith, looking forward to your crown of righteousness.
Let your running be steady.
For it is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God.
Do you not see the portraits of kings, how some of them are large and beautifully adorned?
Others, however, have grown black with time, have deteriorated, and have become objects of ridicule.
This is how all our deeds will be revealed in that place, like portraits.
Let us flee forever from that shame.
Let us also say, “Protect me, Lord, for I have trusted in you,” and, “You have no need of my good things.”
Indeed, he needs nothing among the things that are yours, except only the salvation of our souls.
Therefore, let us offer ourselves up as a living, holy sacrifice, as it is written—not offering ourselves up through fire, but through patience and endurance.
For he said, “The one who endures to the end will be saved.”
And again, “He has toiled forever; he will live to the end.”
Therefore, since we have chosen for ourselves a life free from worry and disturbance,
let us run well so that we may attain the goal, as it is written.
For it is no small danger for us to break the pledge we made with the Lord.
Therefore, let us train our tongue and train our eyes. Let us lift up our hands in holiness, and train our feet to walk uprightly.
Acquire for yourself a good and blameless way of life: humility and modesty,
freedom from disturbance, moderation in eating, strong self-control, love of hard work, compassion, love for others, a willingness to share, and sound faith.
Although all these things seem small when we speak of them in this way, they require a great struggle to put them into practice.

He said, “The kingdom of heaven is like virgins.” He did not say that it is like the sun and the moon and the beautiful host of stars, or gold that will perish, or beauty that fades, or heaven itself.
See the dignity of purity: it ranks above everything.
It was about this that Paul, the bride’s escort, spoke when he said, “But I want you to be free from worry.”
Therefore, we ought to pray that those who are healthy, namely the virgins, may remain in their health.
The sick, too—that is, those who have fallen into sin—will receive healing.
We too ought to weep in this way and wash out our eyes, which have looked upon evil.
You have seen the wound, and you have learned the cure.
Secure the windows of your soul—not only your ears and your eyes and your mouth.
For these are the windows through which the evil one enters, as it is written: “Death has entered through your windows.”
Let the commandments of modesty govern your eyes and your ears.
Let psalms and meditation on the Scriptures be in your mouth.
What we ought to do, then, is open our windows—that is, our senses—to God, and shut them against the enemy.
You too should say with that holy soul, “I will climb a palm tree and grasp its high branches.”
This means: “I will lift my mind to heaven and hold firmly to an upright faith, so that I do not stumble over earthly things.”
But take care, because the palm tree has thorns: these are the rebukes that drive sin away.
For he said, “The words of the wise are like cattle goads and like piercing nails,” so that, as these remain driven into your heart, you may keep yourself away from every sin.
But he said, “Grasp its high branches,” so that you may be up above and have the strength to stand firm under the trials that come upon you.
Read the holy Scriptures regularly, at all times.
For just as wine, when people drink it, soothes sorrow and turns the heart to gladness, so spiritual wine—that is, reading the Scriptures—turns the soul to joy.
Let the [?] of God be in your heart at all times, as you too say with David, “I always saw the Lord before me; he is at my right hand so that I will not be shaken.”
Let these words be written on your hand and firmly fixed before your eyes.
If you honor God by keeping his commandments, he will be at your right hand.
But if you dishonor him through your transgressions, the devil will be at your right hand.
For this is how Scripture testified about Judas when he became a transgressor: “Let the devil stand at his right hand.”
Honor God at every moment, saying, “I will exalt you, my God, my King.”
You are to honor him through deeds, not through words.
This is how David honors him, saying, “I will bless you forever and forever and ever.”
Not for a single day, or a month, or a year, but throughout his whole life.
For he knows that when a person reaches perfection, then he begins in virtue.
But often you will say, “What kind of heart can give glory to God at all times?”
It is a heart like that of the blessed Paul, who writes, “I am not aware of anything I have done.”
And again, like that of David, who says, “Cleanse me, Lord, of my hidden faults.”
It is this kind of heart that the Savior commanded us to acquire for ourselves, saying, “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God.”
This is the condition of the person who does not sin against God.
This is the one who gives glory to God through his words and his deeds.
A person like this will not lose heart, even if sickness, poverty, or death comes upon him.
Instead, he too will say with Paul, “Who can separate us from the love of God?” and the words that follow.
Remember the day [?], that terrifying day, full of [?].
At that time we will stand before the holy judgment seat to give an account of everything we have done, in the place where the sins we have committed will be set before everyone's eyes.
And they will be exposed before those who do not know about them.
In that place are the river of fire and the worm that does not die.
At that time the books of our hearts will be opened, spread out, and read in the midst of that theater.
And all the deeds we have done will be revealed: those done openly and those done in secret, those of the night and those of the day, those we have done carelessly and forgetfully.
Those we have done with the parts of our body, and those we have carried out through the movements of our heart.
At that time we will learn through experience and fact that the things we do in secret will be exposed then.
Remember that we must depart from this place and go before the Judge who cannot be deceived.
He will expose what is hidden in darkness and reveal the intentions of hearts, and he will examine our deeds, our thoughts, and our words.
At that time we will receive great punishments for the sins we have committed, which we think are small.
Remember at all times, and do not forget any flame of Gehenna, which is never extinguished.
Set the Judge before your eyes for a while, the one who is coming to judge the living and the dead.
Think about the thousands upon thousands and the tens of thousands upon tens of thousands of angels standing before the Judge at that time.
Let your ears hear in advance the sound of the trumpets and the terrifying voice of that Judge.
Let your eyes see in advance the things that are destined to happen.
Some are being thrown out into the outer darkness.
But others, after the struggle and hardship of virginity, had the door of the heavenly bridal chamber shut against them.
Look at some being tied up like bundles and thrown into the fiery furnace.
Others are being bound hand and foot and thrown out into the outer darkness.
Some are being handed over to the worm that never sleeps and to the gnashing of teeth.
One is being humiliated because he laughed wickedly and at the wrong time.
Another, because he caused his brother to stumble, or because he violently took what belonged to his neighbor.
Another is being judged for secret sins he committed.
Another is having punishments decreed against him for idle words he spoke.
Another is being condemned for his evil intentions.
Another has the door of the kingdom shut against him because of insults he uttered.
Another has been handed over to unrelenting punishment because of his resentment.
Another has been handed over to everlasting disgrace and shame.
Others have been completely deprived of the knowledge of God. They heard, “I do not know you or where you come from,”
because they engaged in deeds that are abhorrent to Christ.

Since these things are so, what sort of people ought we to be, except to pour down floods of tears every day and say, together with the prophet, “Who will give water to my head and a fountain of tears to my eyes,
so that I may weep over my sins day and night,” so that we may be able to escape the punishment that is to come?
Let us confess our sins beforehand, before that terrifying judgment seat.
Let us appeal to the Lord’s mercies while we are still in this dwelling place.
For he said, “Who will give thanks to you in Hades?”
Let us understand this, my beloved: God gave us all the natural members of our body in pairs.
Indeed, he graciously gave us two eyes, two ears, two hands, and two feet.
If one of these happens to become disabled through illness, we can meet our needs with the other.
But he gave us only one soul. If we destroy it through negligence, how will we live?
Let us therefore take care of it and put nothing above its salvation, because it is the soul that will be made to stand for judgment and give its defense before that judgment seat.
But if at that time you say before the judge, “It was wealth that deceived me,”
The judge will answer you, “Then did you not hear me calling out to you, ‘What will a person gain by gaining the whole world and losing his soul?’”
“Or what will a person give in exchange for his soul?”
He will also say to you, “It did Eve no good when she said, ‘The serpent deceived me.’”
Now then, brothers and sisters, since we have taken these things to heart,
come, let us stir up our own zeal.
Come, let us give glory to God before darkness comes, before that great and manifest day comes upon us.
This is the day the prophet spoke about when he said, “Look, the Lord is coming.”
Who will be able to endure the day of his coming?
That day is terrifying. It is a day of darkness and gloom, a day of clouds and thick darkness, a day of shouting and trumpets.
But perhaps you will say, “Who will be able to escape all these things?”
Listen, and I will teach you.
For do not think that you will be able to escape merely by keeping your body pure.
Rather, when someone does you harm, do him good in return.
When people slander you, conduct yourself wisely in response.
When people curse you, bless them in return.
When you fast, do not become proud. For [?] true fasting is not merely abstaining from food; it is also abstaining from sins.
We ought to search the Scriptures.
For notice that the first thing the prophet saw was a rod of walnut wood.

After that, it was a bronze pot with a fire burning beneath it. This makes the meaning clear: whoever will not endure the rod of discipline here will be tested by the fire of Gehenna in the other place.
In just the same way, Moses was shown a pillar of light and a pillar of fire.
He cries out to everyone, “Whoever obeys the law will enjoy the sweet, true light. Whoever disobeys will be handed over to the fire.”
Read the Gospels and understand that when we leave this world, no one will be able to help us.
No brother will be able to rescue his brother from the unending torments. No friend will be able to help his friend,
nor parents their children, nor children their parents.
And why am I speaking merely about human beings in this way?
For even Noah, Daniel, and Job will not be able to save a son or a daughter.
But you will often say to me, “What is the proof of these words?”
Look at this man who was not wearing wedding clothes, when they threw him out of the wedding feast.
None of those reclining at the table interceded for him.
Look also at the servant who had been given the talent, when they threw him into the outer darkness.
No one pleaded on his behalf.
Look also at the five virgins, when the door of the wedding feast was shut against them.
Their fellow virgins did not appeal to the bridegroom on behalf of these women whom Christ called foolish.
For after they had trampled down the flame of pleasure and quenched the fire of desire,
after many fasts and nights of keeping watch, after sleeping on the ground,
then they were called foolish. And truly, they were rightly given this name, because they had accomplished the great task of virginity,
but had forgotten the small, easy task of kindness toward others.
Picture the judge placing the sheep at his right and the unfruitful goats at his left,
saying to those at his right, “Come and inherit the kingdom.”
But as he throws those at his left out into the outer darkness, none of those at his right could help them.
What he said is true: “Here is the person and his work.”
Have you not heard about that rich man who was hardhearted toward Lazarus, how he longed for a drop of water while he was burning in the place of torment?
You see that Abraham could not save him from the place of torment, even though he begged him.
Therefore, let us help ourselves while we are still here, and give glory to God before darkness comes—that is, before we are banished into darkness.
It is better for our tongues to become dry here through fasting than for us to long for a drop of water in that other place and not be given any.
Let us strive to escape great torments through small hardships here.
Remember that if a fever strikes us for a few days, or if we see people being punished by the judges of this world, trembling and distress seize us,
even though punishment and judgment here last only a short time.
Then what must the punishment of the judgment to come be like, in which we will be punished for endless ages?
Therefore, let us hurry to enter through the narrow gate, and let us not walk through the wide one.
But we know that all the affairs of the world are like dreams, and they are all destined for destruction.
For sickness destroys the body's strength, and beauty, too, fades with old age.
And even if we enjoy a lavish meal, when evening comes we forget its pleasure.
In short, everything here is like cobwebs and dreams.
So the Savior rightly called those who suffer blessed, because the pleasures of this world do not overpower them.
Therefore, just as Abraham heard, “Come out of your land,” let us too come out of our lawless deeds.
And let us pray with Saint David, saying before God, “Seven times a day I have praised you for your righteous judgments.”
For it is a good thing to speak with God at all times through prayer.
For if companionship with a good person changes whoever associates with him for the better, how much more will this happen to someone who speaks with God night and day through prayer!
Who would ever sin while remembering that God is beside him?
Therefore, let us remember the one who said, “Pray at all times,” so that sin may not find a way into our hearts through forgetfulness.
Meditate on death beforehand, and put to death your bodily members that are on earth. The day of the Lord is coming like a thief.
When those who are to take your soul come for you, and you say, “Be patient with me, so that I may fast, give charity, and repent,”
they will say to you, “Did you not hear the Lord crying out, ‘The kingdom of heaven has drawn near’?
“Did you not hear him saying, ‘Show mercy, so that mercy may be shown to you’?
“Did you not hear Paul saying, ‘As long as we have time, let us do what is good’?”
Someone who wants to be saved does not need a long time.
For did the robber need a long time? He only believed, and he gained paradise.
And the holy martyrs inherited the kingdom of heaven in a short time.
They gave their blood; you, for your part, give your tears.
The one who said, “I want everyone to be saved,” does not lie. For this reason, he not only teaches us through the Holy Scripture,
but also teaches us through the misfortunes and sufferings of others.
For we see doctors cutting into people, and rulers sitting on the judgment seat punishing thieves, so that through the sufferings of others we may be corrected.
Now then, my beloved, since we have taken root in faith, let us press onward to knowledge,
and from knowledge into love, and from love to the inheritance in heaven.
Let [?] persevere in prayer, as it is written.
Even when there is no wolf near them, shepherds keep watch at night over their flock of sheep. Even when there is no wild animal, their dogs keep watch beside them.
Therefore it is good for us to conduct ourselves this way at all times, even when no temptation is upon us. Still, this training will not harm you at all; rather, you will benefit all the more.
For who would not benefit from keeping watch at night through prayer?
Therefore we must be watchful in every way, so that no evil may settle in our soul.
For if a soul comes to taste sin and persists in insensibility, it greatly aggravates the sickness of sin.
For just as a spark of fire, when it catches in wood, burns it on every side,
so too is the nature of sin: if it continues to rule over the soul’s thinking, it destroys the entire soul, and the body along with it.
Therefore we must reject sin at its beginning, turning it back like an unruly horse.
If we will have to give an account for an idle word, how much more for the sins that lead to death!
Do not let the sweetness of this life’s affairs deceive us.
For human affairs are no different at all from dreams and shadows, and they pass away like flowing water.
Do not admire possessions and wealth, but look at how they pass from this person to that person, and from this other [?] to yet another.
Therefore we must look down on them.
For the written saying is more than sufficient: “The things we see are temporary, but the things we do not see are eternal.”
Those things do not fade or perish. They are not subject to change.
Let us therefore be eager to acquire these things for ourselves.
Let us strive for these things, for we cannot acquire any of them for ourselves once we have departed from this life.
For athletes do not receive a crown if they abandon the contest. Therefore let us seize the crown for ourselves and escape shame and loss.
For he said, “The one whose work is burned up will suffer loss.”
What, then, will this fire that comes upon us be like?
What, then, will the outer darkness be like?
What, then, will the spirit of weeping and gnashing of teeth be like?
Take these things to heart, and guard your soul, keeping it a virgin until the bridegroom comes in his glory.
You too, sing a psalm, saying, “My soul is always in my hands, and I have not forgotten your law.”
And say, “You are the one who will save me from the fowlers’ snare.”
Let your lamp remain burning. Do not let them find you negligent.
Even if sleep seems sweet to you at night, understand that nothing is sweeter than the psalms.
For the holy man said, “Your words have become sweet to my palate, sweeter than honey in my mouth.”
The martyrs give their own lives for the name of God.
Let us, for our part, offer our ascetic discipline.
Remember that burning coals were spread beneath the martyrs.
You, for your part, must not consider sleeping on the ground a hardship.
If your mouth becomes foul and bitter from fasting, remember that the one who made the sweetness of honey tasted bitterness for your sake.
Even if you have wept once over your sins, you have not yet become like Paul, who wept over the salvation of others.
Let us therefore encourage one another with these words: suffering lasts only a short time, but rest is everlasting.
Overcome suffering through hope.
For he said, “Affliction produces endurance, and endurance produces hope, and hope does not bring shame.”
Reflect that pleasure lasts only a moment, but punishment is everlasting.
Reject the sweetness of pleasure because of the anguish of punishment.
Do not let the devil use our limbs as arrows. Guard yourself; do not let him pierce you with the arrow of gluttony.
For you know that after the people crossed the sea, they did not drown; yet Moses himself is on the ground because of gluttony.
Look at their suffering and flee from the way they fell.
If God did not spare the branches—that is, those people—he will not spare you either if you are negligent.
If, then, you struggle with all your heart, with a sound faith, you will rejoice in everlasting joy and gladness.
Therefore pay attention at all times to these teachings, which are full of salvation, and keep them.
And carry them out, so that the Holy Trinity may be glorified in you: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, now and always, forever and ever. Amen.
Apa John, Archbishop.
